title: JavaScript Object Model: Prototypes, new, Classes, and this
description: Trace property lookup through the prototype chain, explain constructor/new behavior, and choose the right this binding.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish an object's internal prototype link from Constructor.prototype.
Trace property lookup and identify own vs inherited properties.
Explain the conceptual steps of new and class methods on prototypes.
Use private fields and inheritance deliberately.

blocks.text: Objects delegate property lookup through prototypes

An object can read properties it does not own by following its internal [[Prototype]] link. That link is different from Constructor.prototype: the latter is the object that instances created through new Constructor() may delegate to. JavaScript classes use this prototype model; they do not replace it with a separate classical object system.

blocks.title: Do not confuse these values
blocks.text: obj is an instance. Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) returns its prototype link. Constructor.prototype is commonly linked to instances made by new Constructor(). These values often relate, but they are not generally the same object.

steps.title: Create an object with a prototype link
steps.explanation: dog gets its own name property and delegates lookup to animal. The properties of animal are not copied onto dog.

steps.title: Distinguish own and inherited properties
steps.explanation: name is an own property, but speak is found through the prototype chain. Object.hasOwn tests ownership, while normal property access can find inherited properties.

steps.title: Follow the chain to find the method
steps.explanation: dog.speak is found on animal when lookup does not find an own speak property.

blocks.text: For an ordinary constructor call, new creates an object, links its prototype to Constructor.prototype, calls the constructor with this bound to the new object, then returns an explicitly returned object if there is one or otherwise returns the new object. Class constructors add stricter rules, including requiring new.

items: For obj.method(), this normally refers to obj for that call.
Extracting const method = obj.method and later calling method() loses the object call-site; do not expect this to remain obj.
Arrow functions do not create their own this; they capture it lexically.
call/apply invoke immediately with a chosen this; bind returns a new bound function.
Class instance methods are usually stored on the prototype; arrow-function fields create a function per instance and have different memory/reference trade-offs.

blocks.prompt: For const child = Object.create(parent), where is a property found when child has no own property with that name but parent does?

options.text: It is copied automatically from parent to child
options.feedback: Object.create links a prototype; it does not copy parent properties.

options.text: Lookup follows the prototype chain to parent
options.feedback: Ordinary property access looks for an own property, then follows prototype links when needed.

options.text: JavaScript creates a global binding with that name
options.feedback: Object property lookup does not create global variables.

options.text: It can only be found with JSON.parse
options.feedback: JSON parsing is unrelated to prototype property lookup.

blocks.explanation: Own-property tests and ordinary property lookup answer different questions.

blocks.title: Trace prototype lookup and repair a detached method
blocks.context: Run the examples in a JavaScript runtime and explain the observed results using object-model rules.
instructions: Create an object that delegates to a prototype and prove which properties are own vs inherited.
Create a constructor whose instances share a greet method through Constructor.prototype.
Repair a detached callback so it uses the intended object; choose bind, an explicit parameter, or a suitable arrow wrapper.
Explain the difference between a private class field such as #value and a property named _value.
requirements: Property lookup is traced through the prototype chain.
Instances share a prototype method without copying it onto each instance.
The callback has an intentional and predictable this binding.
The explanation distinguishes language-enforced private fields from naming conventions.
hints: Object.create links an object to a prototype; it does not copy properties.
A regular method's this is usually determined by its call site.
bind returns a new function; call invokes immediately.
successCriteria: Own and inherited properties are distinguished.
Constructor-created instances share a prototype method.
The detached method uses an intentional this value.

blocks.text: Shadowing, mutation, and where a write lands

Reading and writing are asymmetric: a read may find a value higher in the chain, but `child.status = ...` normally creates or updates an own property on `child`. It does not update the prototype’s property. This is useful for per-instance overrides, but surprising when a shared prototype value is an object: mutating `child.settings.theme` can mutate the same nested object shared by every instance. Put per-instance mutable data on each instance instead.

steps.title: Reads can be inherited
steps.explanation: Neither instance owns status or settings; both read the same values through defaults.

steps.title: A direct assignment shadows
steps.explanation: The assignment creates first.status. second still reads defaults.status because its own property was not changed.

steps.title: Nested mutation follows the shared reference
steps.explanation: first.settings resolves to the object stored on defaults, then mutates that object. second sees the changed theme. Clone or initialize mutable per-instance data to avoid this coupling.

blocks.prompt: After `const child = Object.create(base)`, what does `child.count++` do when `base.count` is an ordinary writable data property and child has no own count?

options.text: It increments base.count because the original value was inherited
options.feedback: Property access finds the inherited number, but the subsequent ordinary assignment targets child.

options.text: It creates child.count with the incremented value and leaves base.count unchanged
options.feedback: The read is inherited; the write creates an own property (assuming ordinary writable data-property semantics).
Updating a property value does not replace [[Prototype]].

options.text: It throws for every inherited property
options.feedback: Writable inherited data properties can be shadowed. Accessors and non-writable descriptors have different behavior.

blocks.explanation: Always reason about the read and write phases separately; accessors and property descriptors can change assignment behavior.

blocks.text: A property descriptor determines whether a property is writable, enumerable, or configurable, or instead is an accessor with a getter/setter. Prototype lookup can invoke inherited getters, and assignment can invoke setters. For user-controlled keys such as `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype`, avoid merging arbitrary input into ordinary configuration objects without validation. Prefer allowlisted keys or a `Map`; a null-prototype dictionary created with `Object.create(null)` also has no inherited names, but lacks ordinary object methods.

blocks.prompt: You need a dictionary keyed by untrusted user-provided strings. Which design is the safest default among these options?

options.text: Merge every key into `{}` with Object.assign
options.feedback: Ordinary objects inherit from Object.prototype and unsafe merge logic can interact with special keys.

options.text: Use an allowlist or Map, and validate any values before storing them
options.feedback: Explicit keys avoid prototype-chain surprises; Map is designed for key/value collections, while an allowlist limits accepted input.

options.text: Use `for...in` and assume every enumerated key is own
options.feedback: for...in can include enumerable inherited properties; use ownership checks when appropriate.
Strict mode does not make arbitrary object-key handling safe.

blocks.explanation: The prototype chain is part of normal property semantics, so input-key handling must account for inherited names and special merge behavior.

blocks.title: Diagnose an inherited-state bug
blocks.context: A settings panel unexpectedly changes every profile after one profile is edited. Trace property ownership and repair the data model.
instructions: Run the shadowing walkthrough and record own-property checks before and after each assignment.
Create a Profile constructor or class where each instance receives independent nested settings.
Add a test that edits one instance and proves a second instance remains unchanged.
Use Object.getPrototypeOf and Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor to inspect where a property comes from.
requirements: Explain the inherited read versus own-property write behavior.
Show the shared nested-reference failure before the repair.
Give each instance independent mutable settings in the repaired version.
Tests check values and ownership, not only printed output.
hints: Object.create shares the prototype object; it does not deep-clone nested data.
A shallow spread can copy a nested reference without cloning that nested object.
Check both Object.hasOwn(instance, 'settings') and object identity.
successCriteria: Reproduces and explains the shared nested-object bug.
Provides each profile its own nested settings object.
Includes an assertion proving instances are isolated.
Uses descriptor/prototype inspection to support the diagnosis.

items: Property lookup delegates through [[Prototype]]; Constructor.prototype is a separate concept.
new creates an instance linked to Constructor.prototype and initializes this for the constructor.
For regular methods this depends on the call site; arrows capture this lexically, call/apply invoke, and bind returns a bound function.
Use private fields and inheritance intentionally, based on encapsulation and substitutability needs.
